strengths: Significance: FT-Dojo addresses a useful problem: jointly automating data construction and training configuration through evaluation feedback. Its 13 tasks across five domains cover substantially different adaptation requirements.

Methodology: The sandboxed environment, common interfaces, fixed hardware and time budget, and explicit separation between validation feedback and blind test evaluation provide a sensible benchmark foundation.

Empirical promise: Table 2 reports substantial gains over OpenHands on several tasks, including molecule editing (53.33% versus 40.00%), fact checking (83.33% versus 66.67%), and novelty classification (41.09 versus 28.44 Macro-F1). Matching the agent backbone and providing training/evaluation wrappers to OpenHands are valuable controls.

Presentation and originality: The main workflow is clearly explained. The strongest original contribution is the integration of heterogeneous data selection, synthesis, training, and iterative diagnosis into a common evaluation environment. Dataset descriptions, prompt outlines, and failure traces provide useful supporting detail.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript openly presents unsuccessful optimization trajectories and recognizes potential misuse in sensitive domains. These disclosures are valuable; no concrete material ethical violation is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness—uncertainty is not measured. No repeated-run results, confidence intervals, or variability estimates are reported despite stochastic agents, synthesis, and training. AIME's 13.33% corresponds to only two correct answers among 15 test problems; the visualization improvement over OpenHands corresponds to three additional successes among 25. These results do not establish the claimed significant or consistent superiority, and Appendix C's assertion that the AIME difference is not stochastic is unsupported.

Soundness—the proposed mechanisms are not isolated. Section 4.3 varies data volume, backbone, and target-model size, but never removes structured memory/planning, fail-fast validation, or feedback analysis. Consequently, the results do not establish which components cause the gains or increased iteration throughput. A matched one-shot synthesis-and-SFT baseline would also help distinguish benefits of strong teacher-generated supervision from iterative agent optimization.

Baseline fairness remains inadequate for the human-expert claim. Appendix B restricts Manual SFT to two training passes, whereas FT-Agent averages 8.77 loops. Its described workflow uses rule-based cleaning, without establishing equivalent access to synthesis models or comparable human effort. The comparison therefore does not support broad superiority over expert fine-tuning. OpenHands is more carefully controlled, but its custom staged harness also limits conclusions about general-purpose agents as a class.

Evaluation specifications contain material ambiguities. Appendix A.3 caps validation/test allocation at 100 per benchmark or subtask, while larger task totals require a clearly specified finer subdivision; A.4 additionally describes AIME as having 100 examples per split, contradicting Table 1's 15. Accuracy aggregation is insufficiently documented to reconcile, for example, Finance's reported 67.53% with its stated 100-example test set. Appendix A equates visualization Pass@1 with executable-code rate, although Table 5 reports them separately. Exact split manifests, aggregation rules, and evaluator definitions are necessary for a benchmark contribution.

Several central interpretations exceed the evidence. The 'outperforms on 10 of 13 tasks' claim includes a tie on PI4PC, and molecular understanding has mixed metric outcomes. Nonzero AIME accuracy does not prove valid synthesized reasoning or exclude memorization. Appendix G explicitly instructs CoT generation and quality-first processing, weakening claims of discovery without explicit instruction. Selected failure traces, particularly hedging language, cannot establish a fundamental absence of causal reasoning; Table 7's PI4PC trajectory also ends at 34%, without explaining its relationship to the main validation result of 40%.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript provides no code/artifact access statement, exact split seeds, complete executable prompts and configurations, or judge rubrics despite relying on proprietary APIs and customized wrappers. Claimed rigorous decontamination is not accompanied by a reproducible overlap-detection procedure. Table 3's 'iterative only' costs do not establish total synthesis, evaluation, API, and GPU costs.

Originality and reach need tighter calibration. The strongest novelty is the benchmark and workflow integration; the agent components are familiar engineering practices whose distinctive value requires stronger controlled evidence. The absolute claim that no prior work tackles end-to-end agentic fine-tuning needs a more precise comparison with the cited LaMDAgent. Testing two sizes within one model family on five ablation tasks also does not establish model-agnostic generality. These evidential and reproducibility gaps outweigh the benchmark's clear promise.

strengths: Significance: FT-Dojo addresses a useful problem: evaluating agents that jointly construct training data and configure fine-tuning. Its 13 tasks across five domains extend evaluation beyond a single dataset or fixed training pipeline.

Soundness: The stated protocol separates agent-accessible validation feedback from a hidden test set (Appendix F). FT-Agent and OpenHands share the reasoning backbone, target model, GPU, and wall-clock budget, providing useful experimental controls.

Empirical promise: Table 2 reports substantial improvements over OpenHands on prior-art retrieval (70.34 versus 50.51 F1), molecule editing (53.33 versus 40.00 accuracy), and table fact checking (83.33 versus 66.67 accuracy). These results warrant further investigation.

Presentation and ethics: The three-stage workflow is understandable, and the appendices provide data sources, prompt outlines, and informative failure traces. The impact statement acknowledges harmful adaptation risks; the inclusion of unsuccessful trajectories is valuable.
weaknesses: Soundness—uncertainty is inadequately assessed. No repeated-run results, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are reported despite stochastic agent search and very small evaluation sets. AIME's 13.33% represents only two correct answers among 15 test problems; visualization's 36% versus 24% represents nine versus six successes among 25. These observations cannot establish the claimed significant superiority or exclude stochastic variation, as Appendix C asserts. The headline ten-task win count also includes a tie on PI4PC and mixed outcomes across molecular-understanding metrics.

Soundness—the proposed mechanisms are not ablated. Section 4.3 changes data budget, backbone, and target-model size, but never removes structured memory, fail-fast validation, or feedback diagnosis. Consequently, the attribution of improved exploration to these individual mechanisms is unsupported. A fixed synthetic-CoT pipeline and simpler search baselines would also help distinguish the contribution of agent orchestration from strong-model data generation.

Baseline fairness is incomplete. Manual SFT is limited to two passes (Appendix B.1.2), while FT-Agent averages 8.77 loops; the manuscript does not demonstrate that these restrictions equalize compute or access to synthesis resources. The OpenHands baseline uses a custom staged harness and version 0.14, and its description alternates between identical fine-tuning primitives and operating without specialized primitives. These ambiguities weaken claims about superiority over human experts and general-purpose agents.

Reproducibility and reporting need substantial clarification. The manuscript does not provide an implementation artifact, exact split identifiers and seeds, complete executable prompts/configurations, or the stated judge rubric. Appendix A.4 describes AIME as following a 100-example-per-split allocation, whereas Table 1 specifies 15. Appendix A.1.5 equates visualization Pass@1 with executable-code rate, although Table 5 reports them separately. The PI4PC case trajectory peaks at 34% validation accuracy, versus 40% in Tables 8–9, without explaining its relationship to the main experiment. These issues impede reconstruction of the evaluation.

Several central interpretations exceed the evidence. Nonzero AIME accuracy does not prove valid reasoning synthesis or rule out memorization, especially with closed-model teachers and no reported contamination audit beyond source-split filtering. Likewise, selected failed trajectories and hedging words such as 'likely' do not establish a fundamental absence of causal reasoning; cautious language can be appropriate. The cross-domain mixing examples lack matched controls, and experiments on two sizes of one model family do not establish model-agnostic generality. The concern is unsupported inference, not the honest discussion of limitations.

Originality and practical significance are insufficiently established. The benchmark integration is potentially useful, but FT-Agent largely combines familiar planning, memory, validation, and feedback practices. The categorical claim that no prior work tackles end-to-end fine-tuning needs a more precise comparison with the cited LaMDAgent post-training optimizer. Practical efficiency is also incompletely characterized: Table 3 reports only iterative API cost, omitting a complete accounting of synthesis, judging, and GPU expenditure.

strengths: Significance: FT-Dojo addresses a useful problem: evaluating agents that jointly construct training data and configure fine-tuning. Its 13 tasks across five domains provide a broader testbed than a single-domain demonstration.

Originality: The main contribution is the integration of a shared heterogeneous data repository, iterative training, and structured evaluation into an interactive benchmark. FT-Agent offers a practical combination of experiment memory, progressive validation, and feedback analysis.

Soundness: The stated protocol separates agent-visible validation feedback from a hidden final test set. Matching FT-Agent and OpenHands on the reasoning backbone, target model, hardware, and wall-clock budget provides meaningful experimental control. Reported gains on patent retrieval, fact checking, and molecular editing are promising.

Presentation and limitations: The workflow is understandable, and the appendices provide dataset sources, additional results, prompt descriptions, and informative failure traces. The discussion acknowledges unsuccessful optimization and planning failures, while the impact statement appropriately recognizes potential misuse of automated fine-tuning.
weaknesses: Soundness—insufficient uncertainty analysis: No repeated-run statistics, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. Several evaluation sets are very small: the headline AIME improvement represents two correct answers out of 15, and Visualization improves from six to nine successes out of 25 versus OpenHands. These results cannot establish the claimed consistent superiority or rule out stochastic variation, as Appendix C asserts.

Soundness—central mechanisms are not isolated: Section 4.3 varies dataset size, backbone, and target-model size, but never removes experiment memory, fail-fast validation, or structured feedback. Consequently, the paper does not establish which proposed mechanisms produce the gains. A matched fixed pipeline using the same synthetic-data models and CoT instructions is also needed to distinguish benefits of iterative orchestration from benefits of stronger supervision.

Baseline fairness: Appendix B restricts human experts to two training attempts, whereas FT-Agent averages 8.77 loops. Equal wall-clock resources do not justify this additional restriction, and equivalent access to synthetic-data assistance is not established for the human baseline. The OpenHands description also needs reconciliation: B.2.1 says it lacks specialized fine-tuning primitives, while B.2.2 and the main text describe shared wrappers. These issues weaken claims of superiority over expert practice and general-purpose agents.

Evaluation specification and reproducibility: The manuscript does not provide a benchmark implementation link, exact split identifiers/seeds, complete judge prompts, or sufficient scoring details to reproduce the tables. Finance accuracy of 67.53% is not directly explained by the stated 100-example test set; molecular-editing accuracy similarly requires clarification of subtask aggregation. Appendix A.4 describes a standard 100-example split for AIME despite Table 1 reporting 15. Decontamination is asserted without an operational procedure. These ambiguities are material for a benchmark contribution.

Unsupported interpretation: Sections 4.2 and 6 treat nonzero AIME accuracy as proof of valid synthesized reasoning and evidence against memorization, without auditing generated rationales or teacher-model contamination. Appendix G explicitly instructs CoT generation, limiting claims of discovery without explicit instruction. Similarly, selected traces and hedging words such as 'likely' do not establish a fundamental causal-reasoning deficit; calibrated uncertainty is not evidence of absent causal reasoning.

Significance and originality are overstated: The broad claim that no prior work tackles agentic end-to-end fine-tuning needs sharper differentiation from LaMDAgent, which the paper itself cites. Testing two sizes within the Qwen2.5 family supports limited transfer, not model agnosticism; the 3B AIME result remains zero. Claims about a necessary frontier backbone are also mixed: GPT-4o matches AIME test performance and improves Finance in Table 8.

Efficiency evidence is incomplete: Table 3 reports only 'iterative' API cost, without total synthesis, evaluation, or GPU costs. More completed loops within a fixed budget is useful evidence of throughput, but does not by itself demonstrate overall cost efficiency. Together with the missing component ablations and uncertain evaluation results, these gaps prevent acceptance despite the promising benchmark direction.

strengths: Significance: FT-Dojo addresses a useful evaluation gap by treating data construction, training configuration, and iterative diagnosis as joint agent responsibilities. The 13 tasks across five domains provide meaningful diversity beyond conventional fixed-dataset optimization.

Soundness: The stated protocol separates validation feedback from hidden test evaluation and matches autonomous systems on hardware, tools, data access, and wall-clock budget. Comparisons with frontier agents and three independent FT-Agent runs strengthen the empirical contribution.

Empirical utility: Table 2 reports substantial improvements on several tasks, including molecule editing (54.44% versus OpenHands' 40.00%) and fact checking (81.25% versus 66.67%). These results suggest practical value for specialized orchestration.

Presentation and originality: The architecture and workflow are understandable, and the principal novelty is a useful integration and benchmark formulation. The manuscript appropriately acknowledges the constrained human baseline, limited model-scale coverage, and agent failures. Its impact statement recognizes misuse risks without claiming that automation is inherently safe.
weaknesses: Soundness and reproducibility: Evaluation counts and scores require reconciliation. Appendix A.5 explicitly describes FinanceIQ as a monolithic 100-example test set, yet single-run accuracy values include 65.10% and 67.53%. Table 4 reports Codex Visualization Pass@1 of 26% despite a 25-example test set. Such values require an undocumented aggregation or evaluation procedure. Appendix A.1.5 also equates Visualization Pass@1 with executable-code rate, whereas Table 7 reports them as distinct metrics. These ambiguities materially undermine confidence in the benchmark's central measurements.

Soundness: The experiments do not isolate the three proposed mechanisms. Section 4.4 varies data volume, planning backbone, and target model size, but does not remove structured planning, fail-fast validation, or feedback analysis individually. Consequently, claims attributing iteration throughput and performance gains to particular mechanisms remain untested. A synthesis-enabled simple iterative baseline would also help separate orchestration benefits from the strong data-processing models.

Statistical evidence: Baselines and focused comparisons use single runs, while several evaluation sets are very small. AIME has only 15 test questions, so the highlighted 11.11% mean represents fewer than two correct answers per run. Visualization has 25 examples, and FT-Agent's 29.33±6.11% overlaps the vicinity of OpenHands' 24%. Three FT-Agent runs alone do not establish reliable comparative rankings or justify statements that differences are not stochastic.

Reproducibility: The supplied manuscript ends its implementation-availability statement without a link. The appendices provide useful workflow summaries but omit exact split identifiers/seeds, context-filter thresholds, complete executable configurations, and sufficiently precise model/API settings. The claimed rigorous decontamination is not supported by an explicit cross-source overlap audit. These omissions are especially consequential for a benchmark contribution.

Interpretation: The causal-reasoning conclusions exceed the case-study evidence. Appendix D.3 treats hedging language as evidence of pattern matching and attributes a successful intervention to associations in the agent's pretraining data without testing that explanation. Appendix G explicitly instructs the agent to generate CoT, weakening the claim that discovering missing CoT demonstrates an emergent diagnostic capability. The observed traces support descriptions of behavior, not these stronger cognitive explanations.

Efficiency and resource accounting: Table 3 reports only 'iterative' dollar cost without defining its coverage or accounting for all synthesis, cleaning, judging, and GPU costs. The 2,000-instance limit is also insufficiently specified across repeated iterations. Equal wall-clock limits support a bounded-runtime comparison, but the evidence does not establish overall cost efficiency.

strengths: Significance: Autonomous fine-tuning is a useful benchmark target. FT-Dojo combines data construction, training configuration, execution, and iterative feedback across 13 tasks in five domains. Standardizing this interaction is a meaningful potential contribution even though the underlying datasets are existing resources.

Originality: The principal contribution is the integration of data strategy and training configuration into an interactive evaluation environment. FT-Agent offers a practical baseline combining experiment memory, progressive validation, and structured diagnosis.

Soundness: The stated protocol separates validation feedback from final test evaluation and matches hardware, tools, target models, and wall-clock budgets across autonomous agents. Comparisons include frontier coding agents and alternative planning backbones; three-run FT-Agent statistics are more informative than a single trajectory.

Presentation and limitations: The main workflow is understandable, and the appendices provide dataset sources, prompts, evaluation rubrics, and illustrative trajectories. The authors acknowledge the constrained human baseline, unsuccessful optimization trajectories, and limited model-scale coverage. The impact statement appropriately recognizes potential misuse; I see no demonstrated material ethical violation.
weaknesses: Soundness—evaluation results do not consistently reconcile with the specified sample counts. Appendix A.5 explicitly states that FinanceIQ has 100 test examples, yet single-run accuracies include 65.10%, 64.73%, and 67.53%. Table 4 reports Codex visualization Pass@1 of 26.00% despite only 25 test examples. These cannot be ordinary empirical accuracies under the stated denominators. Undocumented aggregation or repeated sampling could explain them, but the manuscript must specify this and reconcile the tables before its comparisons are reliable. Appendix A.1.5 also equates visualization Pass@1 with executable-code rate, whereas Table 7 reports them as different metrics.

Soundness—the central explanation for the AIME result is confounded by explicit instructions. Section 4.2 attributes success to autonomously diagnosing missing reasoning supervision. However, Appendix G.1 instructs the agent to use strong models for CoT generation, G.2 requires all training data to contain step-by-step reasoning, and G.3 treats missing CoT as a hard failure. This supports the usefulness of an expert-specified recipe, but does not establish autonomous discovery of the bottleneck. A baseline supplied with the same CoT requirement is needed to distinguish these explanations.

Soundness—the proposed mechanisms are not directly ablated. Section 4.4 varies dataset size, planning backbone, and target-model size, but never removes structured planning, fail-fast validation, or feedback analysis individually. OpenHands also uses a custom staged harness (Appendix B.2), so its comparison changes several factors simultaneously. The results establish a system-level comparison, not the claimed causal attribution to particular mechanisms or a fundamental cognitive disparity.

Statistical evidence is insufficient for the strength of the ranking claims. Baselines and frontier-agent comparisons have single runs, while FT-Agent has three. AIME has only 15 test questions, so its 11.11% mean represents roughly one or two successes per run; visualization has only 25 examples. Training-run standard deviations do not capture uncertainty from these small test sets. The five-task comparison additionally uses a 'representative' FT-Agent run without specifying its selection rule. Matched repetitions and example-level uncertainty are needed to support robust superiority.

Reproducibility remains incomplete for a benchmark contribution. The manuscript does not supply exact split identifiers or seeds, filtering thresholds, sufficiently precise metric aggregation rules, or full executable configurations. The asserted rigorous decontamination is not accompanied by a concrete cross-source overlap audit. Table 3's costs explicitly cover only iteration, leaving total synthesis, evaluation, and compute costs unclear. These omissions make independent reconstruction and resource comparisons difficult.

Originality and interpretation: The orchestration mechanisms are familiar engineering practices, so their scientific value depends on convincing empirical understanding. Several interpretations exceed the evidence: Appendix D attributes gains to cross-domain data mixing without a matched in-domain-only ablation, and treats hedging language and selected failed trajectories as evidence of deficient causal reasoning. These are useful observations, but do not establish the proposed mechanisms. Overall, the promising benchmark concept does not outweigh the unresolved evaluation inconsistencies and unsupported central explanations.

strengths: Significance: FT-Dojo addresses a useful gap by evaluating autonomous data construction, training configuration, execution, and iterative diagnosis together. The shared repository, standardized interfaces, and 13 tasks across five domains could provide valuable infrastructure for research on autonomous fine-tuning.

Methodology: The stated protocol separates validation feedback from hidden final testing and matches autonomous systems on target model, hardware, tools, and wall-clock budget. Comparisons with Codex and Claude Code, alternative planning backbones, and three FT-Agent runs strengthen the evaluation beyond a single general-purpose baseline.

Originality: The main contribution is a fine-tuning-specific interactive benchmark and an integrated orchestration framework. Combining structured planning, progressive validation, and feedback analysis is practically motivated, even though the individual mechanisms are familiar.

Presentation and limitations: The workflow is generally understandable, and the appendices provide dataset descriptions, prompts, and illustrative trajectories. The authors appropriately acknowledge constrained human comparisons, restricted model scales, and unsuccessful agent behavior. The impact statement recognizes misuse risks; no concrete material ethical violation is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: Reported scores cannot readily be reconciled with the declared evaluation protocol. Appendix A.5 specifies a monolithic FinanceIQ test set of 100 examples, yet single-run accuracies include 65.10%, 64.73%, and 67.53%, which cannot arise from ordinary accuracy on 100 examples. Table 4 reports Codex Visualization Pass@1 of 26% despite a 25-example test set. Appendix A.1.5 also equates Visualization Pass@1 with executable-code rate, whereas Table 7 reports them separately with substantially different values. Exact denominators, aggregation rules, repeated-generation settings, and evaluator definitions are needed to establish what the headline results measure.

Soundness and causal attribution: The claim that FT-Agent autonomously diagnoses missing reasoning supervision is confounded by its instructions. Appendix G explicitly tells it to use strong models for CoT generation, requires all training examples to contain step-by-step reasoning, and treats missing CoT as a hard validation failure. The corresponding guidance is not documented for competing agents. The AIME results therefore do not isolate autonomous diagnosis from supplied expert prescriptions. A baseline receiving the same substantive guidance is necessary.

Methodological evidence: Section 4.4 varies dataset size, planning backbone, and target-model scale, but never removes structured planning, fail-fast validation, or feedback analysis individually. Consequently, the proposed mechanisms' contributions remain unidentified. More completed iterations support the framework's practical utility, but do not establish that fail-fast validation specifically causes the gain or that improved cognitive architecture explains the comparisons.

Statistical support: Only FT-Agent receives three-run statistics; competing agents and the focused comparisons are single runs. AIME has just 15 test problems, so the reported 11.11% mean represents approximately one or two correct answers per run. Visualization has only 25 test examples. Seed variability does not quantify uncertainty from these small test sets, and the five-task advantage over Claude Code lacks uncertainty estimates. The repeated 'best on 10 of 13 tasks' claim also needs a defined task-level rule for ties and mixed outcomes across chemistry metrics.

Reproducibility: The abstract's implementation-availability statement has no accompanying link in the supplied manuscript. The paper does not supply exact split identifiers/seeds, complete executable evaluator specifications, or sufficiently precise agent/API configurations to resolve the reporting ambiguities. The claimed rigorous decontamination is described mainly through official-split removal and filtering, without a reproducible cross-source overlap audit. These omissions particularly affect a contribution whose central value is a reusable benchmark.

Interpretation and reach: The case studies demonstrate interesting behavior, but do not establish the stronger claims about causal reasoning or the origin of successful interventions. Hedging language is not evidence of deficient causal reasoning, and improvement over an untuned model does not isolate the benefit of cross-domain data mixing. The human baseline's two-pass restriction and lack of LLM assistance further limit conclusions about practical superiority, although the manuscript appropriately acknowledges those constraints. Overall, the benchmark idea is promising, but unresolved evaluation inconsistencies and attribution gaps prevent acceptance.
